# Education in Pakistan
Education in Pakistan follows a national system inspired largely by the English model and is divided into stages including pre-school (ages 3–5), primary (years 1–5), middle school (years 6–8), secondary (years 9–12), and tertiary education. Primary education completion stands at about 67.5%, but net primary school attendance is low at around 66%. The curriculum typically covers eight core disciplines including arts, sciences, languages (Urdu and English), religious studies, and Pakistan Studies, with instruction offered in Urdu, English, or regional languages. Secondary education culminates in standardized examinations administered by regional Boards of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE), leading to certifications such as the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and Higher Secondary School Certificate (HSSC). Alternative paths like the General Certificate of Education (GCE) and technical/vocational education also exist, with diploma routes in various engineering and commercial fields.
Tertiary education offers bachelor’s degrees (pass and honours), along with professional and graduate programs in fields like engineering, medicine, law, and education. However, only about 6% of the population hold university degrees, with efforts underway to increase this. Challenges include gender disparity, with female enrollment and literacy rates significantly lower than males, socio-economic barriers, outdated curricula, poor infrastructure, and teacher shortages. While madrasas provide religious education and social support, they are criticized for focusing heavily on rote learning. Recent reforms aim to improve quality, inclusion, and teacher training, and distance learning initiatives have been expanded especially during crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Literacy rates have improved over the decades, reaching around 60% overall in 2023, but remain uneven across provinces and genders. Pakistan hosts a significant number of international schools, reflecting diverse educational demands.
